specAnchors.text: know that an alloy is a mixture of a metal and one or more elements, usually other metals or carbon
explain why alloys are harder than pure metals

primer.text: From Extraction & Uses of Metals you have seen steel types doing jobs that pure iron cannot. This note explains why: alloys are mixtures whose different-sized atoms spoil the tidy atomic pattern of a pure metal, making the layers harder to slide. It also names brass, the classic copper-zinc alloy.

modules.title: Alloys
modules.opening: Alloys are mixtures: a metal combined with one or more other elements, usually other metals or carbon. Steel, for example, is iron mixed with carbon. The blend often behaves very differently from the metals inside it: it can be stronger and harder, and it resists corrosion and extreme temperatures better. These enhanced properties are why alloys often beat pure metals in real uses.
keyPoints: Alloys are mixtures: either several metals together, or a metal with a non-metal such as carbon.
Steel is made from iron mixed with carbon.
Alloys are often stronger and harder than the metals they contain.
Many alloys resist corrosion or withstand extreme temperatures.
Brass, a common alloy, contains 70% copper and 30% zinc.

low.restatement: An alloy mixes a metal with other metals or with carbon, and the mixture often outperforms the original: harder, stronger, and better at resisting corrosion or heat. Brass, with copper and zinc, is the classic example.
low.analogy: Alloying is like blending two fruit juices: the result tastes different from either ingredient, and sometimes nicer.
low.examPointer: Definition questions want the mixture idea plus the examples: steel from iron and carbon, brass from copper and zinc.

medium.restatement: An alloy is a deliberate mixture of a metal with other elements, usually metals or carbon, chosen because the blend outperforms the pure metal. Steel shows the principle with iron and carbon, and brass with seventy percent copper and thirty percent zinc; the enhanced hardness, strength and corrosion resistance make alloys more useful than their ingredients.
medium.analogy: Think of a sports team: individual players are good, but the blended side, with different strengths on the pitch, wins more often than any line-up of identical players.
medium.examPointer: Diagram questions ask you to spot the alloy: choose the picture with unevenly sized particles and distorted rows.

modules.title: Why alloys are harder than pure metals
modules.opening: Pure metals pack their atoms into neat, regular rows, and those rows slide easily over one another when a force is applied. Alloying spoils the pattern: atoms of different sizes distort the regular arrangement, so the layers can no longer slip smoothly. That is why alloys are harder than the pure metals they come from.
keyPoints: The atoms in an alloy come in different sizes.
The different sizes distort the regular arrangement of atoms in the metal.
Distorted layers make it more difficult for the atoms to slide over each other.
Layers that cannot slide easily make the alloy harder than the pure metal.
Diagram questions show the alloy as uneven particles sitting in distorted rows.

low.restatement: Different-sized atoms wreck the neat rows of a pure metal lattice, so the layers jam instead of sliding. Jammed layers mean a harder metal, which is the whole point of alloying.
low.analogy: It is like mixing pebbles of many sizes into a stack of identical marbles: the pile no longer rolls smoothly, and the shape holds firm.
low.examPointer: The explanation chain is examinable: different sizes, distorted arrangement, layers cannot slide, so the alloy is harder.

medium.restatement: In a pure metal the identical atoms form a regular lattice whose planes slip over one another under force, which is why pure metals are soft. Adding atoms of a different size distorts that lattice, so the planes no longer slide freely and the alloy holds its shape, appearing markedly harder than its parent metal.
medium.analogy: Picture a carpet that slides easily on a polished floor; scatter grit of mixed sizes under it and the carpet grips, exactly as foreign atoms grip the metal's planes.
medium.examPointer: Choose-the-diagram questions reward pattern spotting: uneven particle sizes with bent rows identify the alloy every time.

glossary.definition: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually other metals or carbon.
The common alloy containing 70% copper and 30% zinc.
The gradual chemical attack on a metal, such as rusting, that alloys resist better than pure metals.
The regular, repeating arrangement of atoms in a solid metal.
The spoiling of the regular atomic arrangement caused by atoms of different sizes.

workedExample.prompt: a) Define an alloy and give the composition of one named example. b) Explain why brass is harder than pure copper. c) A particle diagram shows unevenly sized atoms sitting in distorted rows. What does it represent?
steps: a) An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, usually other metals or carbon; brass contains 70% copper and 30% zinc.
b) In pure copper the atoms are all the same size in regular rows, so the layers slide over each other easily and the metal is soft.
In brass the different-sized zinc atoms distort the regular arrangement, so the layers can no longer slide easily — the alloy is harder.
c) It represents an alloy: uneven particle sizes with distorted layers are the alloy's signature in diagram questions.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) A mixture of a metal with other elements; brass = 70% Cu / 30% Zn. b) Different-sized atoms distort the layers and stop them sliding. c) An alloy.
